Welcome to lesson ten, edit live! Dash v has a second superpower: edit files on your PC, and the container sees the change right away. You'll use it to work on a web page.
Step one. Let's make a page on your PC. These commands run on your PC, not in a container.
Make dir, my site, creates a folder called my site in your home folder.
Then echo writes a small page, a heading that says Hello from my PC, into index dot H T M L inside that folder. Just like in lesson six.
Now check what's in the file. You've used this command before. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's cat, home folder slash my site slash index dot H T M L. And there's our heading: Hello from my PC.
Step two. Let's mount this folder into a container with dash v.
Start engine x named web on localhost port eighty eighty, as before, plus dash v. Share my site as engine x's page folder. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.

It's docker run, dash d, dash dash name web, dash p, eighty eighty colon eighty, dash v, home folder slash my site, colon slash user slash share slash engine x slash H T M L, and engine x. As in lesson eight, your PC comes first. Then the folder inside the container where engine x looks for pages, which you saw in lesson six.
So the same folder is seen from both sides. It's not a copy: the container sees the same folder as your PC.
Step three. Open localhost port eighty eighty in your browser.
And there it is: Hello from my PC! Engine x is serving the file from your PC. No welcome to engine x page this time.

Getting four oh three forbidden instead? You probably mistyped the folder on your PC. Docker doesn't complain: it silently creates a new, empty folder with that name, owned by root. Engine x finds no page there, and answers four oh three.
The fix: delete the container with docker R M dash f web, remove the wrong empty folder with sudo R M dir, and run again with the right name.
Here's a question. Where did the engine x welcome page go? The image has its own index dot H T M L, and a fifty x dot H T M L, in that folder.
Your folder is placed on top of the container's folder, and hides what the image had there. Let's look inside.
Docker exec web, L S, slash user slash share slash engine x slash H T M L. It lists just one file: index dot H T M L.
Only your file. Fifty x dot H T M L is hidden. But the image itself didn't change: without dash v, you'd get the welcome page again.
Step four. Now the fun part: edit the page on your PC.
On your PC, with no exec and no container, replace the text in index dot H T M L with Changed on my PC. You know how to write a file with echo. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's echo, a heading that says Changed on my PC, into home folder slash my site slash index dot H T M L. Now reload the browser, and the new heading shows up right away. No restart, no exec.
And you don't have to use echo. You can also edit the file in any editor on your PC, like VS Code or gedit.
Step five. Engine x only needs to read your page, but right now the container could also change or delete your files. Let's add colon R O, for read only, at the end of dash v, so it can't.
First, delete web in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
Docker R M, dash f, web. Gone.
Now run it again, the same as before, but with colon R O at the very end of the dash v part.
The page still works. Colon R O only limits the container: it can read the folder, but not change it.
Let's test it. We'll go inside web, and try to overwrite the page with a heading that says Hacked, like in lesson six.
Open a shell inside web. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
Docker exec, dash i t, web, bash. You're now inside the container.
Now overwrite index dot H T M L with the Hacked heading. Pause, type it, then continue.
Echo the Hacked heading into slash user slash share slash engine x slash H T M L slash index dot H T M L. And bash answers: read only file system. Refused! The container can only read the folder.
But you can still edit the page on your PC, and the browser shows the change as before.
Now leave the shell. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
It's exit. So remember: if a container only needs to read a folder, mount it with colon R O. Then a bug, or an attacker inside the container, can't damage your files.
Step six. Time to clean up.
Delete web in one command. Pause the video, type it yourself, then continue.
Docker R M, dash f, web. The container is gone.
But deleting the container doesn't touch my site. Your folder is still here. Keep it, because we'll use it again in lesson seventeen.

Wonderful, your page now lives on your PC! Dash v shares a folder from your PC with the container. Edit on your PC, and the container sees it right away. Add colon R O to mount it read only. And docker R M deletes the container, never your folder. Next up, lesson eleven: settings with environment variables. See you there!
